source: Hollan, Hutchins and Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research
finding: Two principles define the theory. First, the unit of analysis is set by functional relations among elements, not by skin or skull. Second, cognitive events are not all inside individuals: they include manipulating objects and traffic in representations. Three kinds of distribution: across people, between internal and external structure, and through time (earlier products change later events).
numbers: No numbers. Conceptual paper with selected earlier studies.
quote: A process is not cognitive simply because it happens in a brain, nor is a process non-cognitive simply because it happens in the interactions among many brains.
limits: Position paper for HCI. It says the theory is a perspective on all cognition, not a kind of cognition.
agent_relevance: Gives the license for treating model + program + checks as one system: the unit is set by functional coupling, not by what is inside the weights.

source: Hollan, Hutchins and Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research
finding: Core principles listed as guides for what to observe: people establish and coordinate structure in their environment; coordination takes effort to maintain; people offload effort to the environment whenever practical; social organisation gives better load balancing.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Principles are stated, not tested in this paper. Offloading is called a general tendency, with no boundary conditions given.
agent_relevance: Maintenance cost of coordination is a warning: every external store or check the agent uses must be kept in step with the model state.

source: Hollan, Hutchins and Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research
finding: Central hypothesis: the cognitive and computational properties of systems can be accounted for by the organisation and propagation of constraints. The theory rejects a gulf between inside and outside that must be bridged by transduction into internal symbols (the Card, Moran and Newell view).
numbers: No numbers.
quote: the cognitive and computational properties of systems can be accounted for in terms of the organization and propagation of constraints
limits: Stated as a hypothesis; no formal model or test is given in this paper.
agent_relevance: Supports a design view in which constraints (code checks, state files) are propagated between model and program rather than 'read in' as text.

source: Hollan, Hutchins and Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research
finding: Airspeed example. Hutchins' ethnography found pilots use the round dial as a material anchor for a space of meaningful speeds and rarely think of speed as a number. All current glass-cockpit airspeed tapes (Airbus, McDonnell Douglas, Boeing, Fokker) lost the features pilots used. The newest cockpit (Boeing 737-700) copies the old dial in digital form.
numbers: Four manufacturers named; no counts of pilots or flights in this paper.
limits: Claim rests on ethnographic observation, interviews and training participation; no controlled test. Eye-movement experiments were only proposed.
agent_relevance: Design lesson: replacing a representation with a 'cleaner' one can delete the property that carried the computation. Changing the agent's written state format needs the same care.

source: Hollan, Hutchins and Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research
finding: Proposed research loop: principles guide ethnography; ethnography suggests experiments and designs; designs create new workplaces to study. An experiment is described as just another socially organised setting. Cognitive ethnography is event-centred and treats video and interaction logs as primary data.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: The authors say the integrated programme had never been assembled before. Ethnographic inference is under-constrained, which is why they want experiments.
agent_relevance: Suggests logging full interaction traces of the agent system as the main data, then running targeted experiments on hypotheses from the traces.

source: Hollan, Hutchins and Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research
finding: Summary of Kirsh's space studies: spatial arrangements simplify choice, simplify perception, and simplify internal computation. Data came from videos of cooking, assembly and packing, everyday observation, and Tetris experiments. Examples: laying parts in assembly order encodes sequence; grouping jigsaw pieces helps discrimination; striking spaghetti on a table sorts by height.
numbers: No counts given in this paper; authors say the main conjecture was 'strongly confirmed' but findings are 'not easy to summarize'.
limits: Self-reported summary of earlier work; no effect sizes. The full Tetris evidence is in Kirsh and Maglio 1994 (see later lines).
agent_relevance: Maps to O6 (choose the written form): arrangement of working state is itself computation, not just storage.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19, 265-288
finding: Takes the whole cockpit as the unit of analysis and asks the usual cognitive questions (what is represented, how are representations transformed and propagated) of that larger system. Memory for approach speeds is held in speed cards, speed bugs on the dial, speech between pilots, and pilot memory together. Method: cognitive ethnography, 100+ flights observed, simulator video and audio, pilot's own training courses (MD-80 procedures as exemplar).
numbers: Over 100 flights as observer; in all observations never saw a crew fail to compute and set approach speeds (a 'killer item').
quote: the cognitive properties of such distributed systems can differ radically from the cognitive properties of the individuals who inhabit them
limits: Account is 'somewhat stylized'; the paper gives no raw observation tables and no error rates. Procedures from one airline's MD-80 manual.
agent_relevance: Core template: ask what each component stores, for how long, in which medium, and how the state moves. Apply to model, scratch files, tests.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19, 265-288
finding: Speed bug argument. A bug does not enhance pilot memory; it reconfigures the functional system. Without a bug the pilot must remember the target speed, read the scale and compare. With the bug set, the task becomes a judgment of spatial adjacency between needle and bug. The computation is done in a quiet phase and saved.
numbers: No numbers; qualitative task analysis. Two ASI instruments give a redundant check.
quote: Speed bugs do not help pilots remember speeds; rather, they are part of the process by which the cockpit system remembers speeds.
limits: Interpretive claim. No test that pilots' errors fall with bugs; hedged language such as 'probably' is used for error types (transposition errors).
agent_relevance: Direct analogue: a checked artifact (a test suite, a stored invariant) turns a recall task into a comparison task. The saving comes from the redesign of the task, not from a better memory.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19, 265-288
finding: Media differ in persistence, modality and vulnerability to interruption. Speed card is permanent; speech is ephemeral; bug state is robust and survives interruption; pilot memory has unknown persistence. The system is redundant: redundant storage, processing and checking. Speed bugs also move work across time (compute in low workload, use later) and across people (PNF monitors speed, PF watches path).
numbers: Qualitative. Two pilot roles (PF, PNF); two ASIs; several speed bugs per dial.
limits: Descriptive. No measure of how much redundancy reduces error.
agent_relevance: Design rule: put information that must survive interruption into a durable medium, and give each fact two independent routes (G3 style held-out checks).

source: Kirsh and Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action. Cognitive Science 18
finding: Defines epistemic actions: physical actions that make mental computation easier, faster or more reliable. Tetris players rotate pieces more than the final placement needs. A planning-then-acting model predicts about half the possible rotations (1.5 for a piece with four orientations); the observed rotations exceed this for every piece type. Rotations often start within 400-600 ms and sometimes before 100 ms, before planning can finish.
numbers: Expected 1.5 rotations for a 4-orientation piece; observed above expectation for all zoid types, with 95% CI bars (exact means not read from figure). Rotation onset 400-600 ms; some before 100 ms. Subject count not extracted.
limits: Hard to prove one action is epistemic rather than pragmatic, since a rotation can serve both. Authors say so. A fully cascaded-planning model is ruled out by argument, not by a fitted model.
agent_relevance: Offers a test for our agent: count tool calls that do not advance the answer yet cut later error (probe runs, printouts). Those are the machine version of epistemic action.

source: Kirsh and Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action. Cognitive Science 18
finding: Speed comparison. A zoid can be physically rotated 90 degrees in as few as 100 ms; mental rotation of the same shape is estimated at 800-1200 ms from a Shepard-Metzler style pilot task. Even adding 200 ms for pressing the button, physical rotation is far cheaper. A wrong early rotation costs 75-750 ms to undo (shortest keystroke gap about 75 ms, mean about 250 ms).
numbers: 100 ms vs 800-1200 ms per 90 degree turn; +200 ms button time; false-start recovery 75-750 ms.
limits: The mental rotation figure is from a pilot study; the paper gives it as an estimate. Footnote notes self-priming might shorten second mental rotations. Not a replication-grade experiment.
agent_relevance: Cost model: an action is epistemic when it is cheaper than the internal computation it replaces. Useful as a rule for when the agent should run code instead of reasoning in text.

source: Kirsh and Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action. Cognitive Science 18
finding: Early rotation also exposes information. A zoid falls one square per 150 ms at medium speed and takes about half a second to appear in full. Rotating it shows hidden parts 150-300 ms earlier than waiting. The authors list five epistemic uses of rotation: unearth information early, save mental rotation, ease retrieval, ease identification, ease matching of zoid to contour.
numbers: Fall rate 150 ms per square; emergence about 0.5 s; gain 150-300 ms.
limits: Five uses are conjectures; only some are supported by data in the paper. The retrieval claim (1200 ms vs about 1000 ms with two views) is stated as a prediction, not a result.
agent_relevance: Probing the environment to disambiguate a partial input before committing is the same pattern as querying a test or reading a file before answering.

source: Clark and Chalmers (1998) The extended mind. Analysis 58
finding: Active externalism: external features that are in the loop and playing a causal role in the here-and-now count as parts of the cognitive system. Parity principle: if a part of the world works as a process we would call cognitive were it done in the head, it is part of the cognitive process. Otto (notebook) and Inga (memory) example.
numbers: No data. Philosophical argument.
limits: Philosophical claim, with no empirical test. Critics such as Adams and Aizawa and Rupert were not read this session. Authors admit indeterminate cases (the Internet usually fails the conditions).
agent_relevance: Gives a falsifiable-looking criterion for 'same system': the role the stored item plays in guiding action, not where it is stored.

source: Clark and Chalmers (1998) The extended mind. Analysis 58
finding: Conditions for external storage to count as belief, from the Otto case: (1) a constant in the life of the agent, rarely acted without consulting; (2) directly available without difficulty; (3) automatically endorsed on retrieval; (4) endorsed in the past. Reliable coupling is enough even if there is occasional decoupling, as brains also lapse in sleep or intoxication. Social extension needs 'a high degree of trust, reliance, and accessibility'.
numbers: Four conditions listed; no numbers.
limits: Condition 4 is called 'arguable' by the authors. Conditions are informal, not measured.
agent_relevance: Maps onto our setting: a state file or tool counts as part of the agent only if it is always consulted, cheap to read and trusted. Untrusted checks (G2 flags model self-grading) fail condition 3 for the right reason.

source: Hutchins (2013) The cultural ecosystem of human cognition. Philosophical Psychology
finding: Hutchins states that no experiments could prove or disprove the distributed cognition perspective, because the perspective itself makes no empirical claims; hypotheses inside it (such as extended cognition) can be tested. Unlike extended mind, distributed cognition assumes no centre and no privileged boundary; centres and boundaries are empirical, set by density of information flow.
numbers: No numbers.
quote: there is no series of experiments or set of observations that could prove or disprove the distributed cognition perspective, because the perspective itself makes no empirical claims
limits: Primary-author statement. Critics argue this makes the theory hard to falsify; that criticism was not sourced here.
agent_relevance: Important boundary: 'the agent is a distributed system' is a framing, not a result. Value must be shown by tests of specific design hypotheses.

source: Hutchins (2013) The cultural ecosystem of human cognition. Philosophical Psychology
finding: Computational models of distributed cognition: communities of connectionist networks (Hutchins and Hazlehurst 1991, 1995; Hazlehurst and Hutchins 1998) in which language-like patterns emerge with no teacher. Each pair jointly produces a public structure while each network tunes to it. Formal link: both the lexicon problem and Hinton and Becker's depth-from-stereo problem are solved by methods that incrementally maximise mutual information. Later hypothesis: cultural practices reduce entropy (raise predictability) at all scales.
numbers: No simulation numbers given in this paper. Original simulations not opened.
limits: This is a review of the author's own earlier simulations; results are existence demonstrations, not fits to human data. The entropy-reduction hypothesis is described as an ongoing exploration.
agent_relevance: Closest formal model of a coupled agent plus shared public structure. Mutual information between model output and external state could be a measurable proxy for coupling.

source: Hutchins (2012) Cultural practices, emergent patterns, and collective intelligence (CI 2012)
finding: Describes the community-of-networks work as the first test case: each interaction produces an emergent public structure while each agent adapts. Argues practices live partly in artefacts and the arena, so reading and writing are not wholly inside the reader. Claims the Flynn effect fits this view: IQ tests measure the distribution of functional skills that cultural practice has built.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: The Flynn explanation is offered as belief ('I believe'), not tested. Conference abstract-length text.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that capability is partly in the scaffold. Do not treat the Flynn claim as evidence.

source: Hutchins (2010) Cognitive ecology. Topics in Cognitive Science 2
finding: Roots of the unit-of-analysis argument: Gibson's ecological psychology, Bateson's ecology of mind and Soviet cultural-historical activity theory. Bateson's blind man with a stick: draw the system boundary so that no pathway that carries difference is cut. Wrong boundaries leave phenomena inexplicable.
numbers: No numbers.
quote: The stick is a pathway along which transforms of difference are being transmitted.
limits: Historical and conceptual review.
agent_relevance: Boundary rule for design: do not cut the loop between model output, tool result and next model input when you analyse errors (G2).

source: Hutchins (2009) Expectation and surprise (ALPA Air Safety Forum)
finding: Automation surprises in cockpits are explained as gaps in allocation of pilot attention, not lack of knowledge. Attention on control functions neglects guidance parameters and the reverse. Five described cases of attention on control with neglect of guidance, plus converse cases. Surprise is a relation between an event and expectation, not a property of the event.
numbers: Five worked incident cases; no rates.
limits: Case-based argument from the author's data; no base rates or controlled test. Air France 447 is mentioned only as a worry in 2009.
agent_relevance: The checking part of the system fails when the flow of work steers attention away from it. Checks must be forced by code at fixed points, not left to the model's attention (G5).

source: Distributed cognition (Wikipedia, secondary summary)
finding: Lineage and variants: Roberts 1964, Hutchins 1995, Salomon 1997 (shared cognition vs off-loading), Sutton 2006 (five domains: external tools and symbols, natural environment, social scaffolding, embodied skills, internalised artefacts). Zhang and Norman 1994: three components: embodiment of information in representations, coordination of enaction among embodied agents, ecological contributions to a cognitive ecosystem. Hollan et al. 2000: three kinds of distribution.
numbers: No statistics on the page. Several claims on the page carry verification tags; the mother-fetus model rests mostly on one author.
limits: Tertiary source. Page carries factual-verification tags from 2013 and 2015. Dates and attributions should be checked against primary sources before use.
agent_relevance: Shows the field has no single formal model. Sutton's domains give a checklist of where state can live.

source: Zhang and Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks. Cognitive Science 18
finding: Not opened this session (publisher PDF blocked; archive host unreachable). Known only from secondary summaries: the paper analyses tasks with internal and external representations (Tower of Hanoi isomorphs) and argues task performance depends on how the representation is distributed across the two.
numbers: Numbers not captured. Do not cite any figure from this line.
limits: Source not read; flagged for angle B or a later pass.
agent_relevance: If the Hanoi-isomorph result holds, the form of the external representation changes difficulty. Needs the primary text before use.

source: Vallee-Tourangeau, Sirota and Vallee-Tourangeau (2016) Interactivity mitigates the impact of working memory depletion on mental arithmetic. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications 1:26
finding: Experiment with 52 students adding 11 single digits. Hands-down (low interactivity) vs moving number tokens (high), crossed with saying 'the' aloud (articulatory suppression) or not. Suppression hurt much less with tokens. Maths anxiety predicted the suppression penalty only in the low-interactivity condition.
numbers: N=52. Percent correct (SD): low interactivity 56.0% (27.7) without suppression, 26.9% (31.7) with; high interactivity 63.5% (28.2) without, 44.6% (29.5) with. Interaction significant, F(1,51), p<.05. Decimal digits partly garbled in the text extraction.
limits: Brief report, one lab, one task, lab students. Latency in the low condition rose little with suppression, so some people may not have engaged with the secondary task. Needs replication.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a manipulable external store enlarges effective working memory under load. Analogue: code-held intermediate values protect against context load.

source: Henok, Vallee-Tourangeau, Vallee-Tourangeau (2020) Incubation and interactivity in insight problem solving. Psychological Research 84
finding: Cheap necklace problem. Physical chains (high interactivity) vs pen and paper (low). Experiment 1 (N=63): at Time 1, 12 of 28 (43%) solved with chains, 2 of 35 (6%) with paper. After a 2-week gap, 7 of 16 earlier failures with chains (44%) solved it, vs 5 of 33 (15%) with paper. Experiment 2 (N=55): 14 (41%) vs 4 (15%) at Time 1; after the gap, gains came only when the Time 2 task was high interactivity.
numbers: Exp 1 N=63, Exp 2 N=55. Solve rates as listed. Earlier work cited there: under 3% vs 30% in 10 minutes. Working memory (C-Span) predicted success in both conditions.
limits: Single problem type. Lower diligence in the paper-and-pen condition may explain part of the gap (authors note people gave up sooner). One lab.
agent_relevance: Acting on a material model of the problem raises insight rates. For the agent: running a small executable model of the problem may beat reasoning about it in text.

source: Distributed cognition (Wikipedia) report on interactivity and insight
finding: Wikipedia lists further interactivity work: Vallee-Tourangeau 2015 (cards and tokens improved Bayesian reasoning even in adults), Henok 2020 and Fleck and Weisberg 2013 (support for interactivity in insight), and Chuderski et al. 2021 which it says shows mixed evidence on whether distributing cognition helps insight.
numbers: No numbers on the page. Chuderski paper (Br J Psychol 2021, doi 10.1111/bjop.12442) located but not opened.
limits: Second-hand. The mixed result is the one failure-type finding in this cluster; read the primary before quoting.
agent_relevance: Keep interactivity gains as a hypothesis with a known mixed result, not a rule.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science, 2010-2015. Nature Human Behaviour
finding: 21 high-powered pre-registered replications. 13 (62%) showed a significant effect in the same direction; mean replication effect size was about 50% of the original. Sparrow, Liu and Wegner (2011) 'Google effects on memory', the standard lab result on offloading to search, is one of the 21 studies in the reference list.
numbers: 21 studies; 13 replicated (62%); samples about 5x larger than originals; effect size about 50% of original. Which study failed was not read in the main text.
limits: Only the abstract and reference list were checked here. I did not confirm the outcome for Sparrow 2011; check the supplementary table before saying it failed.
agent_relevance: Offloading-harm claims from small lab studies should be down-weighted by roughly half and not assumed to hold.

source: Gao et al. (2022) PAL: Program-aided language models (arXiv 2211.10435)
finding: Model writes the reasoning as code and a Python interpreter runs it. On GSM8K, PAL (Codex) scores 72.0 vs 65.6 for chain-of-thought (Codex) and 58.8 for PaLM-540B CoT. On GSM-HARD (same problems, larger numbers) CoT drops from 65.6 to 20.1 while PAL falls only to 61.5.
numbers: GSM8K: direct 19.7, CoT 65.6, PAL 72.0. GSM-HARD: direct 5.0, CoT 20.1, PAL 61.5. 13 reasoning tasks.
limits: Codex era models. The Table 1 numbers are as reported by the authors; no seeds or intervals shown.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence for the 'model plus program is one system' frame: the program supplies the arithmetic the model cannot.

source: Gao et al. (2022) PAL: Program-aided language models (arXiv 2211.10435)
finding: Ablation shows the coupling matters. Making the model write the code and also 'execute' it without an interpreter gives 23.2 on GSM8K vs 72.0 with the interpreter. A weak coder (text-davinci-001) does worse with PAL than with CoT; PAL wins once code skill is high enough.
numbers: No-interpreter variant 23.2 vs PAL 72.0 (text says 4.5 points above direct; Table 1 direct is 19.7, a 3.5 gap, small inconsistency in the paper).
limits: Boundary condition: gain needs the model to be able to write correct programs. Authors' ablation is on GSM8K only.
agent_relevance: The gain comes from the external executor, not from code-shaped prompts. Prefer real execution to simulated execution.

source: Nye et al. (2021) Show your work: scratchpads for intermediate computation (arXiv 2112.00114)
finding: Letting the model write intermediate steps into a scratchpad raises accuracy on multi-step computation. Polynomial evaluation: few-shot 8.8% direct vs 20.1% scratchpad; fine-tuned 31.8% vs 50.7%. Predicting code execution on synthetic programs: few-shot 11% vs 26.5%, fine-tuned 20% vs 41.5%. In addition, models without scratchpad fail completely on 9 and 10 digit addition beyond the 1-8 digit training range.
numbers: Polynomial: 8.8->20.1, 31.8->50.7. Execution: 11->26.5, 20->41.5. Addition out of distribution: complete failure without scratchpad.
limits: Scratchpad here is model-written text, not an external executor; the few-shot execution figure used a modified accuracy criterion (the paper says so).
agent_relevance: A written external state is a working-memory extension the model reads back; the model's own text serves as the external representation.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR; arXiv 2310.01798)
finding: A loop that lacks an independent check does not behave like a coupled system. With oracle labels telling the loop when to stop, GPT-3.5 on GSM8K goes 75.9 to 84.3. Without oracle (intrinsic self-correction) it falls to 75.1 then 74.7 and, on CommonSenseQA, from 75.8 to 38.1 and 41.8. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0.
limits: Tested on 2023 models and prompts from earlier papers; the authors also note unfair compute comparisons and prompt design as confounds.
agent_relevance: Matches G2/G3: the external check, not the second model pass, supplies the gain. A model loop alone is not a distributed system in the useful sense.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs can't plan, but can help planning in LLM-Modulo frameworks (arXiv 2402.01817)
finding: Position paper with reported planning results. Alone GPT-4 produces about 12% executable goal-reaching plans. With the external verifier VAL feeding back errors, Blocks World reaches 82% within 15 rounds and Logistics 70%; obfuscated Mystery Blocks World stays near 10%. Travel planning baseline with CoT or ReAct on GPT-3.5-Turbo is 0.7%.
numbers: 12% autonomous; 82% Blocks World after up to 15 backprompts; 70% Logistics; about 10% Mystery BW; 0.7% travel baseline.
limits: Results are cited from other papers (Valmeekam 2023; Gundawar 2024) and are described as preliminary for travel planning. A position paper.
agent_relevance: Generate-test-critique with a sound external critic is the paradigm case of a model + program + check system. Gains depend on the model generating plausible candidates (Mystery BW fails).

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your brain on ChatGPT (arXiv 2506.08872)
finding: Essay writing with an LLM, a search engine, or no tool; 54 participants (18 per group), three sessions plus a fourth swap session, EEG recorded. Session 1: 83.3% of LLM users (15/18) could not give a correct quotation from their own essay vs 11.1% (2/18) for each of the other groups. EEG connectivity patterns differed between groups.
numbers: N=54 (18 per group). Quote failure 15/18 vs 2/18 vs 2/18, LLM group differing at p<.001 in pairwise tests. Session 4 swap group smaller (18 total).
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed at time read. Small samples, essay task, many reported comparisons. 'Cognitive debt' reading is the authors' interpretation.
agent_relevance: Offloading to a fluent partner can leave no memory trace in the human; for our agent the reverse concern is that state written to a store may not be re-read. Use only as a caution.

source: Authors not captured (2025) Cognitive Workspace: active memory management for LLMs (arXiv 2508.13171)
finding: Proposes an agent memory layer built on Hollan-Hutchins-Kirsh and Kirsh-Maglio ideas (epistemic action, external workspaces). Reports 58.6% average memory reuse vs 0% for a RAG baseline and 17-18% net efficiency gain, at 3.3x more operations.
numbers: Reuse 54.52% (4 rounds), 57.1% (10 rounds), 58.8% multi-hop, 59.8% conflict task. Net efficiency 17.3-17.9%. Cohen's d values of 23 to 196 reported. 8 documents, 10 rounds, GPT-3.5-turbo.
limits: Very weak evidence: tiny corpus, GPT-3.5, no task accuracy, an implausible effect size, and 'reuse rate' is the system's own count. Treat as an idea paper, not a measurement.
agent_relevance: Shows how the theory is being quoted in agent papers. Do not rely on its numbers.

source: Clark (2025) Extending minds with generative AI. Nature Communications
finding: Comment piece. Argues humans are 'extended minds', hybrid systems defined across brain, body and tools, and that fear of AI offloading repeats the old Phaedrus fear of writing. Cites studies that online search leaves people overestimating what they know unaided, but calls that a small price. Uses predictive processing: brains learn to store only the cues needed to retrieve from the wider system.
numbers: No data. Cites others (refs 2, 10-12) for the overestimation of unaided knowledge.
quote: hybrid thinking systems defined (and constantly re-defined) across a rich mosaic of resources only some of which are housed in the biological brain
limits: Opinion, by a founder of the thesis, in a comment series on LLMs. No test of generative AI specifically.
agent_relevance: Frames the human-AI case. For one agent the part that transfers is the cue-plus-retrieval pattern: keep keys in context, bodies in the store.
